title: Hazards, perils, losses and valuation
summary: Insurable interest, underwriting and the loss ratio, three hazards, named vs open perils, direct vs indirect loss, construction and loss valuation.
objectives: Explain insurable interest, underwriting and the loss ratio
Tell physical, moral and morale hazards apart
Contrast named vs open perils and direct vs consequential loss
Value a loss: ACV, replacement cost, agreed value and stated amount

scenes.title: Hazards, perils, losses and valuation
scenes.subtitle: How insurers size up a risk, and how they put a dollar value on a loss

beats.text: Property and Casualty Insurance Basics is 20% of your exam, about 30 questions.
beats.say: Property and Casualty Insurance Basics is twenty percent of your exam, about thirty questions.

beats.text: Here's how insurers size up a risk and value a loss.
beats.say: Here's how insurers size up a risk and value a loss.

scenes.title: Insurable interest and underwriting
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: insurable interest; underwriting; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. A; ISO CP 00 10 10 12, E.4.d

items.label: Insurable interest
items.detail: Your financial or legal relationship to what's insured

items.label: Property: at the time of loss
items.detail: You're paid no more than your interest when the loss happens

items.label: Liability: potential legal liability
items.detail: The interest comes from your potential legal liability

items.label: Underwriting
items.detail: Accept the risk? How much insurance? At what rate?

beats.text: Insurable interest is your financial or legal relationship to what's insured.
beats.say: Insurable interest is your financial or legal relationship to what's insured.

beats.text: For property insurance, it must exist at the time of the loss, and you're paid no more than your interest.
beats.say: For property insurance, it must exist at the time of the loss, and you're paid no more than your interest.

beats.text: For liability insurance, it comes from your potential legal liability.
beats.say: For liability insurance, it comes from your potential legal liability.

beats.text: Underwriting decides whether to accept a risk, how much insurance to write, and at what rate. Paying claims is claims handling, not underwriting.
beats.say: Underwriting decides whether to accept a risk, how much insurance to write, and at what rate. Paying claims is claims handling, not underwriting.

scenes.title: Loss ratio
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: loss ratio; expense ratio; combined ratio

beats.text: Underwriters watch the loss ratio: incurred losses divided by earned premium.
beats.say: Underwriters watch the loss ratio: incurred losses divided by earned premium.

beats.text: $50,000 of incurred losses on $100,000 of earned premium is a 50% loss ratio.
beats.say: Fifty thousand dollars of incurred losses on one hundred thousand dollars of earned premium is a fifty percent loss ratio.

beats.text: Add the expense ratio to get the combined ratio. Under 100% means an underwriting profit.
beats.say: Add the expense ratio to get the combined ratio. Under one hundred percent means an underwriting profit.

scenes.title: Three kinds of hazard
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: hazard; physical, moral and morale hazard (adapted from hook mn-mn_core-10)
scenes.hook: Physical = the Property. Moral = the Person's character. Morale = 'Meh': careless because insurance will pay.
items: Physical: a tangible condition, like oily rags stored by a furnace
Moral: dishonesty, or a motive to profit from a loss, like a money-losing business
Morale: indifference, like leaving doors unlocked because insurance will pay
A fire or a tornado is a peril, not a hazard

beats.text: A hazard raises the chance of loss. Physical is the Property, Moral is the Person, Morale is Meh.
beats.say: A hazard raises the chance of loss. Physical is the Property, Moral is the Person, Morale is Meh.

beats.text: A physical hazard is a tangible condition, like oily rags stored next to a furnace.
beats.say: A physical hazard is a tangible condition, like oily rags stored next to a furnace.

beats.text: A moral hazard comes from the insured's character or circumstances, like dishonesty or a motive to profit from a loss. A money-losing business carries more of it.
beats.say: A moral hazard comes from the insured's character or circumstances, like dishonesty or a motive to profit from a loss. A money-losing business carries more of it.

beats.text: A morale hazard is indifference: the insured gets careless because insurance will pay. It's about attitude, not honesty.
beats.say: A morale hazard is indifference: the insured gets careless because insurance will pay. It's about attitude, not honesty.

beats.text: And a fire or a tornado is a peril, not a hazard.
beats.say: And a fire or a tornado is a peril, not a hazard.

scenes.q: After buying renters coverage, a tenant stops bothering to lock her apartment door. This is an example of:
scenes.why: She is careless because insurance will cover the loss. That is morale hazard: attitude, not dishonesty.

beats.text: Try this. After buying renters coverage, a tenant stops bothering to lock her apartment door. Which hazard is that? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Try this. After buying renters coverage, a tenant stops bothering to lock her apartment door. Which hazard is that? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: Morale hazard. She's careless because insurance will pay. Moral hazard would mean dishonesty, like a record of insurance fraud.
reveal.say: Morale hazard. She's careless because insurance will pay. Moral hazard would mean dishonesty, like a record of insurance fraud.

scenes.title: Named perils vs. open perils
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: named perils; open perils; special perils; Heniser v Frankenmuth Mut Ins Co, 449 Mich 155 (1995)

columns.name: Named perils
points: Michigan: the insured must prove coverage

columns.name: Special (open) perils
points: Covers all causes of loss except exclusions
Michigan: the insurer must prove an exclusion applies

scenes.tell: A list of what IS covered means named perils. A list of only exclusions means open perils.

beats.text: Named perils coverage covers only the perils listed. In Michigan, the insured bears the burden of proving coverage.
beats.say: Named perils coverage covers only the perils listed. In Michigan, the insured bears the burden of proving coverage.

beats.text: Special, or open, perils covers all causes of loss except those specifically excluded. It used to be called all risks. In Michigan, the insurer must prove an exclusion applies.
beats.say: Special, or open, perils covers all causes of loss except those specifically excluded. It used to be called all risks. In Michigan, the insurer must prove an exclusion applies.

beats.text: So: a list of what's covered means named perils; a list of only exclusions means open.
beats.say: So: a list of what's covered means named perils; a list of only exclusions means open.

scenes.title: Direct vs. consequential loss
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: direct loss; consequential loss

columns.name: Direct loss
points: Direct physical damage to the property

columns.name: Consequential (indirect) loss
points: Loss of rent, business income, extra expense

scenes.tell: Is it the physical damage itself, or a money loss that follows because of it?

beats.text: A direct loss comes from direct physical damage to the property, like fire charring a kitchen.
beats.say: A direct loss comes from direct physical damage to the property, like fire charring a kitchen.

beats.text: A consequential, or indirect, loss results from that damage: loss of rent, business income or extra expense.
beats.say: A consequential, or indirect, loss results from that damage: loss of rent, business income or extra expense.

beats.text: Ask: is it the damage itself, or a money loss that follows?
beats.say: Ask: is it the damage itself, or a money loss that follows?

scenes.title: Blanket vs. specific insurance
scenes.src: ISO CP 03 21 10 12 (definitions); IRMI glossary: blanket limit; ISO CP 00 10 10 12, F.1.b

columns.name: Specific insurance
points: Each item has its own limit

columns.name: Blanket insurance
points: One limit covers two or more items or locations
Coinsurance applies to the total value under that limit

scenes.tell: One limit for many items is blanket. A limit for each item is specific.

beats.text: With specific insurance, each item, like each building, has its own limit.
beats.say: With specific insurance, each item, like each building, has its own limit.

beats.text: With blanket insurance, one limit covers two or more items or locations, and coinsurance applies to the total value under it.
beats.say: With blanket insurance, one limit covers two or more items or locations, and coinsurance applies to the total value under it.

scenes.title: Six construction classes
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: construction classes (ISO Commercial Lines Manual codes 1 to 6)
items: Frame
Wood or veneer exterior walls
Joisted masonry
Masonry walls; combustible floor and roof
Noncombustible
Noncombustible walls, floor and supports
Masonry noncombustible
Masonry walls; noncombustible floor and roof
Modified fire resistive
Rated 1 hour to under 2 hours
Fire resistive
Rated at least 2 hours

beats.text: There are six construction classes. Code 1, frame, is the least fire-resistive. Code 2 is joisted masonry.
beats.say: There are six construction classes. Code one, frame, is the least fire-resistive. Code two is joisted masonry.

beats.text: Code 3 is noncombustible, and code 4 is masonry noncombustible.
beats.say: Code three is noncombustible, and code four is masonry noncombustible.

beats.text: Code 5, modified fire resistive, is rated at least 1 hour but under 2. Code 6, fire resistive, is rated at least 2 hours, the most fire-resistive.
beats.say: Code five, modified fire resistive, is rated at least one hour but under two. Code six, fire resistive, is rated at least two hours, the most fire-resistive.

scenes.title: Three ways to value property
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: replacement cost; actual cash value; functional replacement cost
scenes.hook: Replacement cost buys it new. ACV blows out the birthday candles: the new price minus depreciation. Functional replacement only has to do the same job.
items: Replacement cost: like kind and quality, no deduction for depreciation
Actual cash value: often replacement cost minus depreciation
It can also be fair market value or the broad evidence rule
Functional replacement: does the same job equally well, need not be identical

beats.text: Now, valuing a loss. Replacement cost buys it new. Actual cash value blows out the birthday candles: the new price minus depreciation. Functional replacement only has to do the same job.
beats.say: Now, valuing a loss. Replacement cost buys it new. Actual cash value blows out the birthday candles: the new price minus depreciation. Functional replacement only has to do the same job.

beats.text: Replacement cost means like kind and quality, with no deduction for depreciation.
beats.say: Replacement cost means like kind and quality, with no deduction for depreciation.

beats.text: Actual cash value is often replacement cost minus depreciation. Depending on the policy and state law, it can also be fair market value or the broad evidence rule.
beats.say: Actual cash value is often replacement cost minus depreciation. Depending on the policy and state law, it can also be fair market value or the broad evidence rule.

beats.text: Functional replacement cost pays for property that does the same job with equal efficiency, even if it isn't identical.
beats.say: Functional replacement cost pays for property that does the same job with equal efficiency, even if it isn't identical.

scenes.title: Actual cash value of a roof
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: actual cash value (example as in hook mn-mn_core-16 and question core-034)

beats.text: Let's work one. A roof would cost $20,000 to replace today and has depreciated 40%. What's its actual cash value?
beats.say: Let's work one. A roof would cost twenty thousand dollars to replace today and has depreciated forty percent. What's its actual cash value?

beats.text: Depreciation is 40% of $20,000, or $8,000.
beats.say: Depreciation is forty percent of twenty thousand dollars, or eight thousand dollars.

beats.text: So actual cash value is $20,000 minus $8,000, or $12,000. Watch out: $8,000 is the depreciation, not the answer.
beats.say: So actual cash value is twenty thousand dollars minus eight thousand dollars, or twelve thousand dollars. Watch out: eight thousand dollars is the depreciation, not the answer.

scenes.title: Agreed value vs. stated amount
scenes.src: ISO CP 00 10 10 12, G.1 (2012 BPP); ISO CA 99 28 03 10, B.1-3 and Schedule note (2010 Stated Amount endorsement)
scenes.hook: Agreed value sends coinsurance on vacation. Stated amount is a ceiling, not a promise: you get the LEAST of ACV, repair cost or the stated amount.
items: Agreed value (2012 BPP option): coinsurance suspended until its expiration date
Stated amount (2010 auto endorsement): pays the least of three amounts
Least of: actual cash value, cost to repair or replace, or stated amount
The stated amount is a ceiling, not a guaranteed payment

beats.text: Don't mix up these two. Agreed value sends coinsurance on vacation. Stated amount is a ceiling, not a promise.
beats.say: Don't mix up these two. Agreed value sends coinsurance on vacation. Stated amount is a ceiling, not a promise.

beats.text: Agreed value is an optional coverage in the 2012 Building and Personal Property form. It suspends the Coinsurance condition until the agreed value expiration date.
beats.say: Agreed value is an optional coverage in the twenty twelve Building and Personal Property form. It suspends the Coinsurance condition until the agreed value expiration date.

beats.text: Stated amount is common for auto physical damage. Under the 2010 endorsement, the insurer pays the least of actual cash value, repair or replacement cost, or the stated amount.
beats.say: Stated amount is common for auto physical damage. Under the twenty ten endorsement, the insurer pays the least of actual cash value, repair or replacement cost, or the stated amount.

beats.text: So you can get less than the stated amount.
beats.say: So you can get less than the stated amount.

scenes.q: Under the 2010 ISO Stated Amount endorsement, a van with a $30,000 stated amount is totaled. Its ACV is $26,000; like-kind replacement is $28,000. Ignoring the deductible, the insurer pays:
scenes.why: Stated amount pays the least of actual cash value, repair or replacement cost, or the stated amount. The least here is the $26,000 actual cash value.

beats.text: Your turn. Under the 2010 endorsement, a van with a stated amount of $30,000 is totaled. Its actual cash value is $26,000, and like-kind replacement is $28,000. Ignoring the deductible, what's paid? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Your turn. Under the twenty ten endorsement, a van with a stated amount of thirty thousand dollars is totaled. Its actual cash value is twenty six thousand dollars, and like-kind replacement is twenty eight thousand dollars. Ignoring the deductible, what's paid? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: $26,000, the actual cash value, because it's the least of the three. The stated amount of $30,000 is only a ceiling.
reveal.say: Twenty six thousand dollars, the actual cash value, because it's the least of the three. The stated amount of thirty thousand dollars is only a ceiling.

items: Property insurable interest must exist at the time of loss
Physical is the property, moral the person, morale is 'meh'
Named perils lists what's covered; open perils lists exclusions
Actual cash value is often replacement cost minus depreciation
Stated amount is a ceiling; agreed value suspends coinsurance

beats.text: To recap: property insurable interest must exist at the time of loss. Physical is the property, moral the person, morale is meh.
beats.say: To recap: property insurable interest must exist at the time of loss. Physical is the property, moral the person, morale is meh.

beats.text: Named perils lists what's covered. Actual cash value is often replacement cost minus depreciation. And stated amount is only a ceiling.
beats.say: Named perils lists what's covered. Actual cash value is often replacement cost minus depreciation. And stated amount is only a ceiling.
